newsitem.title: NORWAY: Arafat urges European, U.S. pressure on Israel.
newsitem.headline: Arafat urges European, U.S. pressure on Israel.

text.p: Palestinian President Yasser Arafat urged the international community on Tuesday to pressure Israel to pull out troops from the occupied West Bank city of Hebron.

"We are not asking for the moon," he told a news conference after meeting Norwegian Foreign Minister Bjoern Tore Godal. "We are asking for what has been agreed upon, for what has been signed, to be implemented."
Ending a two-day visit to Norway, which brokered the now-troubled 1993 Israeli-PLO pact on Palestinian self-rule, Arafat said an Israeli withdrawal from Hebron, delayed since March, was long overdue.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has insisted on modifying security arrangements in a deal reached by Israel's previous Labour-led government with the PLO. About 400 Jewish settlers live in enclaves in Hebron among 100,000 Palestinians.

Asked what could be done to forge agreement with Netanyahu, Arafat said: "There must be international pressure because as you know he gave some promises to some fanatic groups during the election campaign. International pressure must be taken to help both of us to carry on the peace process."
He added: "We are committed completely to what had been agreed and what had been signed. We hope the other side will do the same."
"We need Norwegian, American and European efforts," said Arafat, who was travelling to Dublin in the evening to meet leaders of Ireland, current president of the European Union.
Irish Foreign Minister Dick Spring went to Israel and Gaza this month to lend EU support to the peace process.
Arafat said Russia also had a role to play and he would meet Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Friday either in the West Bank or in Gaza.
Asked when a Hebron pullout could realistically take place, he said: "We hope very soon...It is the biggest Palestinian city and it is very important for us to liberate it."
Godal, who visited Israel and the West Bank earlier this month, said Norway had a particular interest in Hebron where it had about 40 observers.
"There is no solution outside the written agreements. The agreements reached in a written form the basis of the redeployment in Hebron. Full stop," Godal said.
Arafat dismissed Israeli accusations that he was stalling on a Hebron agreement by visiting Norway and said he was in contact with his negotiating team in the Middle East.
"We are in the 20th century," he said. "There are faxes and phones and everything is going smoothly."
